chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruchendur (திருச்செந்தூர், 5 of 6): beside the confessions of bondage to courtesans and the decay of the old body, several songs ask for something higher, the One that the gods seek, the yogi's absorbed vision and the breath's ascent to the nectar of the moon, and others confess the poet's begging at patrons' doors; the praise turns on Valli, Siva taught by his son, and Vishnu as uncle.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (83, 85, 88, 89, 90, 92); the dying or aged body (84, 86, 93); the passing goods of household life (87); begging with poetry (86, 91); songs of inner attainment (81, 82, 94); and 95, mostly a battle of Rama with a short plea for release.

81.reading: The poet asks to be given the One that Indra on his spotted elephant amid the clouds, Brahma who expounds the Vedas, and Vishnu of the discus asleep on the serpent all wander in search of, so that, the waves stilled, he may taste it and grow clear within. The praise names Murugan who rides the ram and dwells in the lotus pool, who gave joy to the young hunter girl, and whose vel shattered the golden peak, at coral-walled Senthil.
81.nuance: ஒன்றைத் தரவேணும்: what is asked for is named only as 'the one', the thing the three great gods fail to find. திரை அற்று, with the waves gone, and தெளிதல், becoming clear, make the goal a stilled and clarified mind. The identifications of the three gods rest on epithets (புகர், புயல், சுருதிச் சங்கப் பொருள், திகிரி) and the first lines are hard to divide.

82.reading: The poet confesses that, wandering in the deceitful play of women with breasts like full cool pots, he lost his wisdom and did not know shame, became base, left his heart unguarded, did no dharma and sank in desire even watching the lives of those who had died; to end that delusion he asks that cause and effect fall away, the self that says 'I' break, both eyes rest on the tip of the nose with breath and fire held, body, speech and heart go one way, and that, thinking of the feet, he shine as a yogi of seeing. The praise names Murugan, full of perfect knowledge, to whom Siva bowed saying 'I am lower', the slayer of Sura risen from the sea in a vast form, and the nephew of Mukunda who hurled the discus at the crocodile when the elephant cried 'Root!', at Seeralaivay where conches give birth to pearls on the sand.
82.nuance: The remedy for infatuation is a yogic programme: யானெனும் மேதை விண்டு (the 'I' broken), நாசியின் மீது இரண்டு விழிபாய (the gaze on the nose tip), காயமும் நாவும் நெஞ்சும் ஓர் வழியாக (body, speech and mind made one). ஆதிரையான் is Siva, whose star is Thiruvathirai; his saying நின்று தாழ்வன் makes the father bow to his son as teacher. A garbled word in line 9 (காலுட லுடி) is unclear.

83.reading: The poet asks that, agitated, grieved, without sense or livelihood, he not lie in the laps of common women who call him with pretended love and bind him; instead, he asks, give your feet to protect me, the title of a poet who sings fine Tamil so that service flourishes, and the renown that comes to the mind. The praise names Murugan who fell at the hunter girl's feet in the millet field, cut off Sura's head and struck the hill, and spoke into the ear of the father of Thiruchitrambalam, apparently the five letters.
83.nuance: The plea asks for honours (புலப்பட்டம், புகழ்ச்சி) but for the sake of service: எனக்குத் தொண்டுறப் பற்றும் புலத்துக் கண் செழிக்கச் செந்தமிழ் பாடும். In 76 the poet's titles are pride; here they are asked for as tools of devotion. சிறக் கற்கும் அஞ்செழுத்து அத் தந்து, if so divided, makes Murugan teach Siva of Chidambaram his own five-letter mantra; the division is uncertain. As in 71, Murugan prostrates before Valli (தெண்டனிட்டு).

84.reading: The poet pictures his death, wife, children and kin wailing, the body burning in the fire, what is left cast into water, and the life in the hand of cruel-eyed Death, and asks Murugan to come so that he, his servant, may worship his victorious feet. The praise names Murugan who went into the forest of lions and tigers and lived with the hunter girl, the one at Senthil whom devotees praise, the ever-young lord whom women with faces like moon and lotus embrace.
84.nuance: The scene runs past the moment of death to the cremation and the casting of the ashes into water (விண்டு புனலில் வஞ்சம் ஒழிய விழ), an unusual length for the plea. ஒரு பாச விஞ்சை விளைவும் அன்று is obscure; it may say that what happens is no work of magic or bond, or be divided otherwise.

85.reading: The poet gives a head-to-foot catalogue of women, cloud hair, crescent brow, bow-like eyebrows, eyes that shame the carp, the bee and the lotus, earrings, pearl teeth, areca-like neck, breasts like hills, coral lips and thighs like plantain stems, and asks whether he will trust these deceivers in eye, hand, foot and act. The praise is a battle in drum syllables with conches and trumpets proclaiming the son of Sambhu, the poet, Kandan, as Sura's host and his hill burn and Indra takes refuge, and names Murugan who delights at Senthil with the girl of the Kurinji hut.
85.nuance: The whole first half is the conventional blazon of beauty, each part matched to its comparison, and the question only comes at the end: செயல் வஞ்சரை நம்புவேனோ. Among Murugan's titles proclaimed by the drums is புலவன், the poet.

86.reading: The poet asks that before Death, his flower-red eyes blazing, raises his club and tears him away, before the kin who live here wear out their love quarrelling 'this is mine, why yours?' over their shares, and before the body passes, Murugan end the sorrow of his base trade of begging with sung Tamil and give him joy. The praise names Murugan who gave the true meaning to Sambhu while Vishnu, conch in hand, slept and Brahma's wisdom failed, who wears the hunter girl's kumkum on his golden arms, at Senthil of moats and sandalwood groves.
86.nuance: இசைக்கும் செந்தமிழ்க் கொண்டு அங்கு இரக்கும் புன்தொழில்: the poet's Tamil is named as the means of his begging, the confession of 69 and 71. The kin dividing the dying man's goods (எனக்கு என்று இங்கு உனக்கு ஏன்று) is a sharp detail. The opening lines on the senses are hard to divide.

87.reading: The poet lists house, gold, sons, beautiful wife, strength, family standing, town and name, youth, ornaments, ranks and kin, and asks whether it is right to take the pleasure of this passing dream as his own, lie with women, join many bodies and fall again into the womb. The praise names Murugan who removes the old deeds of devotees who think of him, whose vel split the great mountain, who stays at Senthil, and who embraced the hunter maiden.
87.nuance: மாயக் கனவுநிலை இன்பம் அதனை எனது என்று கருதி: the error is the claim 'mine' over a dream. The list moves from goods to people to rank, then to women, and ends at the womb (கருவில் விழுகின்றது): attachment's end is rebirth.

88.reading: The poet heaps names on the courtesans: women who open the cloth over scented breasts, whimper at every door, feign a childhood love for old lovers, sell remedies for love-sickness, want whatever wealth comes, coldly drop men without money, have mothers who play the dark-goddess drama, drink palm toddy and mix with the low, and asks whether kinship with them is fitting. The praise names Murugan as the younger brother of the elephant-faced one who wrote the Bharata on Meru, Valli's lover, the nephew of Vishnu who came as a lion and tore open the demon king's chest and wore his entrails, and the lord of the gods given by Sankara, at Senthil.
88.nuance: The catalogue of abuse (மழுங்கிகள், சிணுங்கிகள், வம்பிகள், சண்டிகள், மிண்டிகள், பறம்பிகள், தொண்டிகள், கடம்பிகள்) runs on one suffix, a set feature of the book. அவர் தாய்மார் நீலி நாடகமும் பயில் மண்டைகள: the mothers are part of the trade, as in Naladiyar's courtesan chapter. The praise names Ganesa writing the Mahabharata on Meru and the Narasimha story outright.

89.reading: The poet speaks of women with doe eyes and breasts like golden peaks, whose speech drips like cane juice, who on the flowered bed say 'first give the gold and coins' and, once given, talk as sweet as milk and honey, and asks whether kinship with these fools of pleasure is fitting. The praise names Vishnu, Achyuta, who fought the demon king with bow and arrows, as uncle, Murugan as the son born to Kali for those who have left behind talk sweet as milk, syrup and sugar, and as honey at Senthil where devotees swarm.
89.nuance: பொற்பணம் முதல் நீ தா, ஈந்தால் ... பால் தேன் போல செப்பிடும்: the payment comes first and the sweet words after, the sequence the Kural's courtesan chapter condemns. The rhythm, with long syllables at every foot, splits words heavily and much of the praise is uncertain.

90.reading: The poet lists what the young women show, cloud-like hair, moon-like brow, budding smile, nectar speech, creeper eyes, lotus face, breasts like hills, creeper waist, bangled hands and jewelled hips, and above all the practised arts, and confesses that he wallows in the mire of infatuation with them, without asking for anything. The praise names Murugan the son of Siva who burned Kama's form with a smile, who shows love so that his union with the elephant's maiden never slips, and who showed refuge to Indra on Airavata's back and protected him wholly.
90.nuance: Each line repeats காட்டி, 'showing', so that the women's beauty is a display, and the confession ends without a request: மயலின் சேற்றில் உழல்வேனே. இபமின், the elephant's maiden, is Devayanai, raised by Airavata.

91.reading: The poet asks that, no longer wandering to the doors of fools singing crores of rhythmic Tamil garlands, with past deeds gone and love of women far away, he, the old servant, be ruled by Murugan, who will come at the decisive hour on the golden peacock that dances to the drum. The praise is a long string of titles ending in காரன்: guardian of the Vedic sacrifice, master of Tamil verse, helper of the gods, lord of the cock, lover of those who fold hands over their heads, wielder of the vel that pierced the hill, lover of the elephant's maiden and of the hunter girl, friend of devotees of fine speech, and destroyer of Sura, at Senthil.
91.nuance: முந்து தமிழ் மாலை கோடிக் கோடி ... முஞ்சர் மனை வாசல் தேடித் தேடி: the confession of begging with poetry again, now with the poet's verse called garlands. The praise answers it: Murugan is himself செந்தமிழ் சொல் பாவின் மாலைக் காரன், the one to whom such garlands belong.

92.reading: The poet pictures women with sandal-dressed breasts, smiles, red lips, flowers falling from their hair, spear eyes, tilaka on the brow and beads of sweat on the face, and asks whether he will wander after them, his acts undone. The praise names the vel that opened a way out for the poets shut in the mountain at their fine words, the arms embraced by the hunter girl's breasts, and Senthil, where conches cry from the waves onto the lotus and bees sing.
92.nuance: செயல் அழிந்து உழன்று: infatuation undoes one's own agency, where in 22 the undoing of one's agency was the goal. மலைமுகம் சுமந்த புலவர் செஞ்சொல் கொண்டு வழிதிறந்த செங்கை வடிவேலா points to the story of Nakkirar and the poets held in a mountain cave, freed by the vel when he sang; the text gives the details but not the name.

93.reading: The poet pictures old age, hearing gone, heavy breathing, faltering acts, harsh words, vomiting, phlegm in the nose, and asks that before his life wanders out of its cage, Murugan remove the reality of Death, join him to the golden feet and grant a little grace. The praise names Murugan as guru to Siva who bent the golden mountain against his foes, the one who spoke many sly words to the hunter girl in the forest, the Murugan in whose mouth lies the meaning of the Tamil way, at Senthil of the holy waters.
93.nuance: கூற்றத் தத்துவம் நீக்கி: what is asked is not only rescue at death but the removal of Death's principle. வாய்ப்புற்ற தமிழ் மார்க்கத்து இட்பொருள் வாய்க்குச் சித்திர முருகோனே makes Murugan the master of Tamil's meaning.

94.reading: The poet, who has done no just deed and enjoyed delusion amid the illusions of the five elements, asks when the one day will come when, taking up the root yoga that the gods cannot find, the breath driven fast through the fire, rising to the moon in the head where the nectar of bliss wells, going up through the nadi to the space beyond, he will live where there is neither you nor I nor even the nadi. The praise is given to the goddess, the drinker of poison, Matangi who speaks the Veda, the dark Nili, Chamundi who struck down Death with her feet, the one who dwells in fire, wind and sky, the dancing Kali, partner of the rider of the bull and Vishnu's younger sister, and names Murugan as her son, who went to the towns of his devotees and played there, the peacock hero of Senthil.
94.nuance: The plea is a full account of yogic ascent: வாசி (breath) through அனல் (fire) to மதி (the moon), where the இன்ப அமுது ஊறல் flows, and then மேலைவெளி, the space above. The goal, நீ இன்றி நான் இன்றி, is beyond the duality of devotee and Lord. The praise, nearly all of it on Uma as Shakti, gives her the deed of kicking Death (காலன் விழ மோது சாமுண்டி).

95.reading: Most of the song is a battle: Ravana comes with his army of horses, chariots and elephants, boasts and fights, the monkeys hurl rocks and trees, the demons are torn apart, Yama's messengers drive them south and ghouls feast on flesh and marrow, and Vishnu wins with his arrows. The poet then calls 'refuge, refuge', asks the Lord to give his small mind grace little by little and to grant the house of bliss, at Senthil of ponds full of conches, lotuses and fish.
95.nuance: The plea comes only at the end and is brief: தஞ்சம் தஞ்சம் ... இன்பம் தரு வீடு அது தருவாயே. Uncommonly, the battle in the praise is Rama's against Ravana rather than Murugan's against Sura.

links.note: The Kural puts double-minded women, liquor and dice together as the company of those Fortune has abandoned; 88 joins two of the three in one figure, the courtesan who herself drinks palm toddy.
Both describe the yogi who binds the breath and tastes the nectar of bliss from the moon; Tirumular sets it against the liquor of fools, 94 against a life of delusion and the elements' illusions.
Both catalogue old age through the failing senses, cough and phlegm before death; 68 adds the mocking women and the family, 93 asks for more than rescue, the removal of Death's very principle.
Both confess wandering from door to door of worthless patrons with poems; 91 adds that Murugan himself is the true owner of the Tamil garlands the poet wasted.
76 asks to be rid of the poet's titles and honours as pride; 83 asks for the poet's title and fame, but only so that his service and song to Murugan may flourish.

The Tirumanthiram verse tells how Brahma and Vishnu sought Siva's foot and crown and did not see them (அடிகண்டிலேன், with Brahma lying முடிகண்டேன்). The song names the same gods, with Indra, as wandering in search (திரிய) of a thing it calls only ஒன்றை, and asks that this be given (தரவேணும்); what the gods failed to find by searching is asked for as a gift.

Tirumular says that if both gazes are set on the middle of the nose (நாட்டமும் இரண்டும் நடுமூக்கில் வைத்திடில்) there is no self and no seeking, and one becomes Siva (தானில்லை ... சிவனவ நாமே). The song asks for the same practice, both eyes on the nose (நாசியின் மீது இரண்டு விழிபாய), with the 'I' broken (யானெனும் மேதை விண்டு), as the cure for infatuation: the two texts tie the gaze to the end of the self.

The Kural says that one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு அறுப்பான்) enters a world above the gods'. The song asks that the 'I' break (யானெனும் மேதை விண்டு) and gives a method for it, breath and gaze held and body, speech and heart made one (காயமும் நாவும் நெஞ்சும் ஓர்வழியாக), turning the Kural's renunciation into a yogic practice.

Tirumular describes the town wailing, the name taken away and replaced by 'corpse', the body burned on the burning ground and the mourners bathing and forgetting (நீரினில் மூழ்கி நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). The song runs through the same sequence, kin wailing (வந்து கதற), the body in the fire and what is left cast into water (விண்டு புனலில் ... விழ), but where Tirumular ends on the mourners forgetting, the song turns to the feet it asks to worship.

The Kural's lover says blue lilies, if they could see, would hang their heads, saying they cannot match her eyes (குவளை கவிழ்ந்து நிலன்நோக்கும்). The song's blazon uses the same conceit, eyes that cast shame on arrow, carp, bee and lotus (கணை அம் கயல் வண்டு புண்டரிகங்களையும் பழி சிந்து பார்வை), but the whole catalogue ends in the question whether to trust these deceivers (செயல் வஞ்சரை நம்புவேனோ): the Kural's praise is turned into evidence against the women.

The Kural says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than begging, even water for a cow (நாவிற்கு இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்). The song calls the poet's own trade, begging by singing Tamil (இசைக்கும் செந்தமிழ்க் கொண்டு அங்கு இரக்கும் புன்தொழில்), base, and asks for its disgrace to end: the tongue that sings Tamil is the tongue the Kural says begging shames.

Tirumular says the poor in sense, seeing that even their own shadow does not help them, still sit saying 'this wealth is mine' (என்னது மாடென்று இருப்பர்கள்). The song lists house, gold, sons, wife, rank and kin and calls taking the pleasure of this passing dream as 'mine' (மாயக் கனவுநிலை இன்பம் அதனை எனது என்று கருதி) the error, then follows it to the womb (கருவில் விழுகின்றது): both locate the fault in the claim of 'mine'.

The Naladiyar compares a harlot's love to lamp-light: as the light ends when the oil is gone, their love ends when the hand is empty (அவரன்பும் கையற்ற கண்ணே அறும்). Among the song's charges is the same: the women coldly drop, with love gone, those who have no money (காசிலாதவர் தங்களை அன்பற ... நெகிழ்ந்த), so the song's catalogue contains the Naladiyar's whole verse as one item.

The Kural warns that the sweet words (இன்சொல்) of women who desire wealth rather than love bring harm. The song shows the order exactly: on the bed they say 'first give the gold coins' (பொற்பணம் முதல் நீ தா), and once paid they speak as sweet as milk and honey (ஈந்தால் ... ஆன்பால் தேன் போல செப்பிடும்); the sweet speech is the receipt for the gold.

The Naladiyar says household women cannot dress up their womanliness the way maids do, while the other kind, like a fresh flood, show their charms themselves (புதுப்பெருக்கம் போலத் தம் பெண்ணீர்மை காட்டி). The song is built on the same verb, காட்டி repeated for hair, brow, smile, eyes, breasts and hips, ending in women who show their practised arts (தொழில் அதிகம் காட்டு மடமாதர்): beauty as display is the shared mark of the women both texts set apart.

The Naladiyar says that those with aching hearts who stand begging at the gates of great houses (நெடுங்கடை நின்றுழல்வது) do so as the fruit of former deeds (முன்னை வினையாய் விடும்). The song confesses the same wandering at the doors of fools (முஞ்சர் மனை வாசல் தேடித் தேடி உழலாதே) and asks that the former deeds go (முந்தைவினை ஏவராமல் போக): what the Naladiyar states as fixed consequence, the song asks Murugan to remove.

In 22 the poet asks that his mind melt and his own agency be undone again and again (என் செயல் அழிந்து அழிந்து அழிய) so that he may see Murugan. Here, following women, he fears wandering with his agency undone (செயல் அழிந்து உழன்று திரிவேனோ): the same loss of one's own doing is the goal in one song and the ruin in the other, depending on what undoes it.

The Naladiyar pictures the old whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth, and says that those who still turn to desire have no path to safety (ஏம நெறிபடருமாறு இல்லையே). The song gives the same decay, hearing gone, acts faltering, harsh voice (செவி கேட்பற்று ... செயல் தடுமாறி), and asks at that very stage for the golden feet and a little grace (சற்றருள்): it allows a way the Naladiyar closes, on condition of grace.

source_issues: Song 88: one corrupt character in கி஡ணட (line 23); ஡ண for ரீ, so கிரீட (crown), as in songs 12 and 20.
Song 94: two corrupt characters, in லு஡டு (line 8, probably லூடு, 'through') and லு஡றுங் (line 9, probably லூறும், 'wells up'); also unflagged முலபர (line 6), probably மூலபர.
Song 82: unflagged garble காலுட லுடி (line 9); the second word is unclear.
